search.text: Start with a preview, then install into the profile you choose. fxcss records what it installs, checks for local edits before upgrades and keeps backups when replacing an existing theme. Already have a manually installed theme? Use adopt to bring it under management.
Looking for a theme? Browse the Firefox CSS Store or r/FirefoxCSS, then pass its GitHub repository to fxcss try.

title: fxcss try
description: Test-drive a theme before committing to it. Downloads it, installs it into a throwaway profile, and opens Firefox so you can actually use it. Your own profile…

search.text: fxcss try adamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS fxcss try github.com/owner/theme --with compact-tabs fxcss try owner/theme --info # report what's there, launch nothing fxcss try ~/src/my-theme # a theme folder on this computer

Test-drive a theme before committing to it. Downloads it, installs it into a throwaway profile, and opens Firefox so you can actually use it. Your own profile is never touched — close the window and nothing remains.
It reports what it found before doing anything:

fxcss try AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS ★619 MIT MacOS Big Sur like theme for Firefox on MacOS & Windows. Make your Firefox look like Safari. latest release v2.1.0 (2026-10-28) latest commit 68f8699 (2026-11-10) fix: align the toolbar and close the tab bar gap … fetching release v2.1.0 … layout chrome/ at the repository root 72 stylesheets, 377 KB loads 35 stylesheets 29 browser-window, 2 web-content, 4 shared user hook customChrome.css not shipped, as intended installer install.sh fxcss copies the files itself and never runs it Optional stylesheets 30 · layer any on with --with name,name Tweaks compact-tabs hideextension increase-contrast singletabhidden tabs-swapclose enabletabview highlight-tab noidentity standard-urlbar windows-swapclose Colour schemes · pick one theme-ayu-mirage theme-github-dark theme-nord theme-catppuccin-frappe theme-gruvbox-dark theme-one-dark … Setup beyond the files 1 automatic · 3 to check ✓ automatic 3 prefs in configuration/user.js in fxcss's own block ! check Firefox's native vertical tabs a setting in Firefox's own sidebar options … README install flags as the README words them, for its own script; fxcss never runs it -c Left hand side tab close button -v Re-enables the tabview button -p Makes tabs height compact like… -t <name> Colour theme (see Colour themes below) …

Releases are preferred over branch tips, since that is what the author blessed; --commit takes the latest commit instead, and --ref takes any tag, branch or SHA. A browser URL for a branch or folder (https://github.com/owner/theme/tree/photon-style/themes/one) is read as meaning that branch and that folder, and the branch is then tracked rather than pinned. --with name,name layers on the theme's optional stylesheets so you can see a variant without hunting through install flags. --shot dir captures the standard screenshots instead of opening a window, and --keep dir leaves the download behind so you can start editing it with watch.
How the theme is found
Theme repositories are laid out in more ways than chrome/userChrome.css. try, install and upgrade share one plan for reading a source tree, and say which layout they found:

Layout Example What happens chrome/userChrome.css at the root WhiteSur Safari, ShyFox Used where it is. userChrome.css at the root, parts beside it ArcWTF, Foxlim, the GNOME theme The folder is chrome/; documentation, licences, screenshots and install scripts are left out unless a stylesheet refers to them. Only userContent.css GlassyFox Installed as a content-only theme; the browser window is left alone. One theme in a subfolder firefox/chrome/…, NewFox/profile/chrome/… Found, and the folder recorded so upgrades read the same place. Several themes side by side 1.Normal/, 2.WithTST/; Simplify's colour families A real choice: a menu at a terminal, otherwise an error listing the --subpath values. Folders that look historical (old/, Old Versions/, screenshots) or belong to Thunderbird are listed but not chosen. src/userChrome-<edition>.css files WhiteSur Named editions, chosen with --subpath src/userChrome-WhiteSur.css; a sibling common/ folder is merged in the way the theme's installer does, by copying. A committed chrome.zip Win 7 Aero Unpacked as data within size limits and read like any other tree. .rar/.7z are reported as unsupported with the reason. No entry stylesheet at all Brave-Fox, Firefox-Onebar Unsupported, naming the sheets a README might tell you to @import; --entry path.css generates a userChrome.css that imports one.

The planner never selects a directory outside the download, and nothing from the download is executed: a theme whose entry sheet imports files the source does not contain (Material Fox's uncompiled user-chrome.css) is reported as needing a build rather than installed half-empty. install stops there unless --force; try only warns.

try --info ends with a setup checklist: what the theme needs beyond its files, read from the files it ships and its README — preference files outside configuration/user.js (with their pref names), .uc.js scripts that need a userChrome.js loader, extension settings to import, fonts, forks and platform effects. Each item is required, optional or unknown, with the evidence. Nothing on it is applied automatically; see install --prefs below.
Private repositories, other hosts and local folders

A private repository looks exactly like a missing one to anyone who cannot read it. fxcss sends GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN when either is set; otherwise, if a repository is not publicly visible or an anonymous request hits GitHub's rate limit, it asks the GitHub CLI for its login (gh auth token) and tries again. So after gh auth login, private themes your account can read work like public ones and a signed-in person is never told to sign in. The token is only ever sent to GitHub's own hosts — never to another host, and never across a redirect that leaves GitHub — and never appears in a message.

Themes on Codeberg, git.gay (and other Forgejo instances listed in fetch.HOSTS) and GitLab can be tried, installed and upgraded from their URLs; their public APIs answer the same questions. adopt compares against GitHub's tree API and says so when it meets another host. A repository that has moved on GitHub resolves to its new owner/name, is downloaded from there (the old name still answers on the API but not on the download host) and is recorded under the new name.

A theme that is not on GitHub, or not pushed yet, can be tried from its folder: fxcss try ~/src/my-theme. The folder is read where it is and never modified; --with, --shot and --info work as usual, while --ref and --commit do not apply.
When a repository cannot be read, fxcss says why and what to try next rather than printing a traceback:

error: GitHub has no public repository owner/theme. Check the name at https://github.com/owner/theme If it is private, sign in with `gh auth login` or set GITHUB_TOKEN to a token that can read it. For a theme on this computer, pass its folder instead, such as ~/src/my-theme
It does not run the theme's install script

fxcss installs the theme's files and supported preferences itself. It reports any installer it finds and reads the options documented in the theme's README. A theme that requires additional setup outside those files and preferences may still need manual steps.

What is left is the theme's own content: CSS, SVG, and occasionally a .js file. Firefox does not execute a .js file sitting in a profile's chrome folder; that requires an autoconfig hook in the application directory, which fxcss does not create. Archives are size-capped and path-checked on extraction, and symlinks in them are skipped.
If you decide you want the theme permanently, fxcss install is the same resolution and the same file copying — pointed, deliberately, at your real profile.

title: fxcss install
description: Put a theme into the Firefox profile you actually use — the cross-platform replacement for each theme's own install.sh (and the answer for themes whose install…

search.text: fxcss install owner/theme # into your default profile fxcss install owner/theme --with compact-tabs # optional sheets, permanently fxcss install ~/src/my-theme # a local checkout works too fxcss install owner/theme --subpath 2.WithTST # one of several editions fxcss install owner/theme --prefs user.js # also a shipped preference file fxcss install --list-profiles # see what it found first

Put a theme into the Firefox profile you actually use — the cross-platform replacement for each theme's own install.sh (and the answer for themes whose install script never covered Windows). Resolution is the same as try: a GitHub owner/name or URL with --ref/--commit, or a local directory. As with try, the theme's own install script is never executed.

It finds your real profiles by parsing profiles.ini in the platform's Firefox directory (macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox, Windows %APPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox, Linux ~/.mozilla/firefox plus the snap and flatpak locations) and installs into the profile Firefox itself would open. --profile <name-or-path> overrides; with several profiles and no clear default, interactive runs get a picker and scripts get an error — CI is never prompted. Profiles kept somewhere unusual can be added to the search with FXCSS_PROFILE_ROOTS=/path/to/dir, mirroring FXCSS_FIREFOX_ROOTS.

Firefox's default profile decides only for install, which is choosing where to put a theme. Every command that acts on one already installed — uninstall, upgrade, rollback — looks for the profile that has it, so a theme installed deliberately into your Developer Edition profile is still found by a bare fxcss uninstall. adopt looks for the opposite: a chrome/ folder fxcss did not install. Firefox's default breaks the tie only when more than one profile qualifies, and --profile always wins.

The picker and --list-profiles say which Firefox each profile belongs to, because default-release and dev-edition-default are one word apart in a list of hashed directory names — and installing into the wrong one looks exactly like the theme not working:

Which profile? 3 found in ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles › 1. default-release Release 8f2b1a.default-release (Enter) 2. dev-edition-default Developer Edition c41d9e.dev-edition-default 3. work unrecognised 7ab3.work Which one? ↑↓ or 1-3 [1]
The label comes from the directory suffix Firefox itself assigns, so a profile you named yourself reads unrecognised rather than being guessed at.
Run it without --with and it offers the theme's optional stylesheets rather than leaving you to find them in the repository:

Optional stylesheets 30 · pick any Tweaks 1✓ compact-tabs 5. increase-contrast 9. tabs-swapclose 2. enabletabview 6. noidentity 10. windows-swapclose … Colour schemes · pick one 11. theme-ayu-mirage 21. theme-material-ocean … 15. theme-catppuccin-mocha › 25✓ theme-nord … Include which? ↑↓←→ and space to tick, or e.g. 1,3 or all [1,25]

When a theme ships both, colour schemes (named theme-…, or after a palette such as nord or catppuccin-mocha) are listed apart from the tweaks; any other theme gets one list. The grouping is only how the menu reads: the sheets are numbered straight through, and what you pick is imported in the theme's own order. "Pick one" appears when every pair of the theme's colour schemes clashes in the way described below, so installing any two of them would be refused. Pick two anyway and the menu asks which one to keep:

Keep which colour scheme? both set the same 110 colours; only one can take effect 1. theme-catppuccin-mocha ██ #11111b ██ #cdd6f4 ██ #cba6f7 ██ #6c7086 › 2. theme-nord ██ #242933 ██ #eceff4 ██ #88c0d0 ██ #5e81ac (Enter) Which one? ↑↓ or 1-2 [2]

Each row shows the colours that sheet would set, most-used first, as a swatch in that colour and its hex code (just the hex code where the terminal cannot show the colour). Enter keeps the one that loads last, which is the one that would have won anyway.

Every numbered question answers to the keyboard at a terminal. ↑ and ↓ move the › (← and → cross columns), Space ticks a stylesheet, Enter takes the answer and Esc stops. Typing the number works as it always has, and moves the pointer as you type. Through a pipe, in CI, with TERM=dumb or in a terminal narrower than 60 columns, the question is a plain typed prompt; set FXCSS_PLAIN_PROMPTS=1 to keep it that way everywhere, for example for a screen reader that copes badly with lines redrawn in place. Each question ends by naming the option that skips it next time (--profile, --with, --firefox, --subpath, --ref or --commit).
Options that cancel each other out

Some of a theme's optional sheets are alternatives rather than additions. Installing two colour themes is two @imports, and nothing about that warns you — the later one silently wins outright, leaving a browser that looks like neither the one you picked nor the one before it. install measures for this and stops:

$ fxcss install AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS --with theme-nord,theme-dracula theme-dracula and theme-nord are alternatives, not additions: both set the same 122 declaration(s), so whichever loads last replaces the other entirely :root { --gnome-browser-before-load-background: #282a36 } vs { …: #2e3440 } Refusing to install stylesheets that cancel each other out — only one of them would have any effect, and which one is decided by import order rather than by you. Pick one, or pass --force.

It is a measurement, not a guess about names. Two sheets are alternatives when they set the same properties on the same selectors — provable from their text, and true whatever they are called. Matching on a theme- prefix would be a convention rather than a fact: it would tell a theme shipping theme-blue and theme-compact that those clash when they compose perfectly well, and miss a pair named dark.css and nord.css. Sheets that agree exactly are not in conflict, because two options setting the same border radius the same way compete for nothing.
try reports the same thing and continues — a throwaway profile is a fine place to watch two colour themes cancel out — and tweaks says so before screenshotting a --combo that cannot take effect.

What this does not see. It compares declarations, so it catches sheets fighting over the same property. Two sheets that rearrange the same area through different selectors — WhiteSur's tabs-swapclose and windows-swapclose both move a close button and share no declarations at all — are invisible to it. fxcss tweaks --combo a+b proves those from the rendered pixels — and says so itself: a combo that renders identically to one of its parts alone is called out in TWEAKS.md as not a real combination on that Firefox. Silence from the static check is "nothing measurable", never "verified compatible"; the pixels are the judge.

When the theme's default branch has moved on since its newest release, that choice is put to you as well — a tag can be a year behind a fix you are looking for, and equally the branch can be mid-rewrite, so neither is right to assume:

Which version? the default branch has moved on since the latest release 1. release v2.0 2025-01-03 what the author last published (Enter) 2. latest commit on master 2026-08-14 newer than the release — fix tab colours Which one? 1-2 [1]
Scripts and CI never see any of these prompts: without a terminal the release wins, as before, with a one-line note that --commit exists.
The install is what a theme's install script does, done carefully:
the complete replacement is prepared before your existing chrome/ moves to a timestamped chrome.backup-* sibling; a failed swap restores it;

any --with optional sheets go where the theme's own @imports expect them, or load after the base theme through an import-only wrapper; the local files each sheet refers to (nested @imports, images, fonts) come along to the same relative place, so it looks as it did in fxcss try. Files outside the theme, or where the theme already installed a different file, are not copied, and the install says so;

toolkit.legacyUserProfileCustomizations.stylesheets is enabled in user.js — inside a clearly marked block, so it can be removed cleanly — together with any configuration/user.js the theme ships, whose pref names are listed before you confirm. Everything outside the block is kept byte for byte;

shipped preference files elsewhere (a root user.js, config/user.js, prefs/recommended.js) appear on the setup checklist with their pref names and are not applied unless you say --prefs user.js; then they join the same removable block, as written, and upgrades carry the choice forward (stopping if the file disappears upstream). Nothing is ever applied from README prose or from -moz-pref() toggles in the CSS;

a manifest (chrome/fxcss-install.json) records every file written, its sha256, where the theme came from — which host, repo and ref, whether that ref was a release or a branch, and the full commit a branch pointed at — plus the layout selected, the preference files applied and each optional sheet's path in the repository.

When several options have the same name, select their repository paths, for example --with custom/tabs.css,optional/tabs.css. Each retains its identity through upgrades. Options loaded after the base get separate dependency trees when combined. If two selected files need the same native import slot, or would overwrite different contents already there, installation refuses before changing the profile, including with --force.
Tracked branches are downloaded at the resolved commit SHA, and adoption compares that exact tree. If the full SHA cannot be read, fxcss stops instead of recording a branch name as a known revision.
Installing over a profile fxcss already manages keeps the files you added there active (see upgrade); installing over a chrome/ folder fxcss did not write moves it aside whole, as the origin backup.
Restart Firefox after installation; it reads userChrome.css at startup. See uninstall to remove a theme later.

title: fxcss adopt
description: Most themed profiles were not themed by fxcss — someone ran the theme's install.sh, or copied a chrome/ folder in by hand, long before any of this. fxcss…

search.text: fxcss adopt owner/theme # identify what is already installed fxcss adopt # …if chrome/ says where it came from fxcss adopt owner/theme --ref v2.0.0 # check against one version only

Most themed profiles were not themed by fxcss — someone ran the theme's install.sh, or copied a chrome/ folder in by hand, long before any of this. fxcss profiles can describe those, but nothing can act on them: there is no record of what the theme is. adopt writes that record, and then upgrade, rollback and uninstall all work.

It identifies the theme by its contents. Every file under chrome/ is hashed exactly the way git hashes a blob and compared against the repository's own tree at each recent version. A version where every file matches is not a guess — it is the same bytes:

$ fxcss adopt AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS fxcss adopt default-release profile default-release ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/8f2h1kqp.default-release comparing 148 files against AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS … v2.0.0: 129/135 files match, 6 edited, 7 added v1.6.3: 114/132 files match, 18 edited, 10 added best match: v2.0.0: 129/135 files match, 6 edited, 7 added Recorded as that version plus local differences, so an upgrade knows not to overwrite them without being told. backup the theme as it is now, kept as chrome.backup-20260817014143 yours 7 files that version does not ship, kept as your own across upgrades ✓ Recorded 135 files as AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS@v2.0.0 fxcss upgrade can now update it, and fxcss uninstall puts this back.
Files in chrome/ that the matched version does not contain are recorded as yours, not the theme's: upgrades carry them across and uninstall leaves them where they are.

Comparison uses GitHub's git-tree API rather than downloading anything, so checking ten versions costs ten small requests instead of ten archives — and archives are the first thing GitHub rate-limits.

Naming the repository is usually necessary. adopt checks chrome/ for a git remote (definitive — someone cloned it there) and for GitHub URLs in the theme's own files (a hint worth confirming), but plenty of themes leave no trace at all once installed: WhiteSur's chrome/ contains no URL anywhere. That is normal, not a failure, and the message says so. A repository that was only mentioned — a credit, a palette, an upstream — is recorded only when at least half of a version's files match; otherwise adopt refuses and asks you to name the repository yourself, because recording the wrong project hands every later upgrade to it.

A match against a branch records the commit the branch pointed at, not its name, so upgrade --check straight after adopting an exact branch tip says "up to date" instead of announcing the same commit as an update.

Nothing is installed or replaced. The chrome/ already there is copied to a chrome.backup-* and then described, so uninstall has somewhere to put things back to — verified as a byte-identical round trip. user.js is left exactly as it is: the pref that turns userChrome.css on is evidently already set, since the theme is working, and writing an fxcss block to say so again would edit a file for no gain. The next upgrade writes one properly, from the theme it fetches.

Files that already differed from the release are recorded, and upgrade treats them exactly like edits made after an install — it will not overwrite them without --force. That matters here more than anywhere: a theme someone has been hand-editing for a year is the most likely thing to be adopted.

Two versions can also be identical in content while differing in line endings, which is what a Windows clone with core.autocrlf produces. That is reported as a match, noting the difference, rather than as "nothing matches".

title: fxcss profiles
description: Read-only. Firefox keeps its profiles in directories named after a hash, so it can be hard to tell which profile has the theme by looking at folder names.

search.text: fxcss profiles # what is themed where fxcss profiles --check # …and whether anything newer exists fxcss profiles --json # machine-readable
Read-only. Firefox keeps its profiles in directories named after a hash, so it can be hard to tell which profile has the theme by looking at folder names:

$ fxcss profiles --check fxcss profiles Firefox profiles 2 in ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles ● default-release Release 8f2h1kqp.default-release theme AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS @ v2.0.0 installed 2026-08-14 09:12 tracking the release sheets theme-nord files 145 ! 1 edited since install, 1 added by hand update v2.1.0 available 2026-10-28 dev-edition-default Developer Edition p93kd0zx.dev-edition-default theme ! installed by hand chrome/ holds 41 files fxcss adopt takes it over; fxcss install would replace it, backing it up first ● opens by default: the profile Firefox opens on its own

Three states, kept distinct on purpose: a profile fxcss installed into and can speak for, a profile with a chrome/ folder someone put there by hand, and a profile with no theme at all. Only the first can be described in detail; for the second, all fxcss honestly knows is that files are there and that installing would move them aside.

--check asks the host once per theme, not once per profile, and compares like for like: an install tracking releases is measured against the newest tag, one tracking a branch against the commit that branch points at now (a branch other than the default is looked up by name). An install pinned with --ref reports as pinned rather than as behind. A release-tracked install that is current while the default branch has moved on says both — and stays on releases; upgrade --commit is the way to follow the branch instead. Where the manifest predates fxcss recording which of those applied, it says so instead of guessing — "up to date" is never printed unless it was actually checked.

The same reservation covers local edits: installs from before 0.16 recorded no file hashes, so fxcss profiles reports them as not checked for edits rather than as unmodified. Reinstalling records them.

title: fxcss upgrade
description: upgrade updates the installed theme, not Firefox itself. It re-installs the theme the profile already has, at whatever is newest of the kind it tracks: an…

search.text: fxcss upgrade # take the newest version of what you have fxcss upgrade --check # report only; exit code says what it found fxcss upgrade --audit # check the new version against your Firefox first fxcss upgrade --compare # see it before deciding: installed vs new, rendered fxcss upgrade --ref v2.1.0 # somewhere specific fxcss rollback # …and back again

upgrade updates the installed theme, not Firefox itself. It re-installs the theme the profile already has, at whatever is newest of the kind it tracks: an install that took a release moves to the newest tag, one that followed a branch moves to that branch's current commit, and one pinned with --ref does not move at all unless you say so.
It stops rather than surprise you, in four places:
Files you edited yourself. Every install records a sha256 per file, so an upgrade knows which ones you have since changed and refuses to write over them until --force.

Files you added. A stylesheet you dropped into chrome/ — imported from customChrome.css, say — is carried into the new tree so it stays active, not merely kept in the backup where it would stop applying. customChrome.css itself counts as yours once you have written in it, even though fxcss created the empty file. The manifest lists them under user_files. If the new version ships a file at the same path with different contents, that is a collision: the upgrade stops before anything moves and lists the paths; --force installs the theme's copies and leaves yours in the backup, recorded as displaced.

Options that vanished. If you installed --with theme-nord and the new version renamed or dropped that sheet, the @import would simply stop resolving and the option would turn itself off. upgrade names the loss and makes you choose instead. Sheets are matched by their path in the repository first, so a sheet that only exists inside chrome/extras/ survives an upgrade as reliably as one in custom/. The same goes for preference files chosen with --prefs.
Selectors the new version needs and your Firefox lacks — with --audit, which runs the same check as fxcss audit against the fetched copy before anything is installed.

--compare renders what is installed and what the upgrade would install — the profile's own chrome/, local edits and carried-over sheets included, not a re-fetch of what the manifest says — and diffs them before the confirmation prompt, printing where the before/after images landed. It completes the three questions an upgrade can answer about a theme with no API: do the selectors still exist (--audit), has the user edited anything (always checked), and what actually changes on screen (--compare). Needs a local Firefox, like shot.

--check changes nothing and answers with its exit code, for cron, launchd or CI: 0 up to date, 1 an upgrade is available, 2 it cannot be told (no install here, an unreachable repo, or a manifest too old to say what it tracked). For a theme installed from a local folder there is no upstream to ask, so the folder's files are compared with what was installed and "up to date" includes the managed preference block. Explicit --prefs and --with choices can also change an installation whose remote revision is current; --check reports whether that proposed setup differs without applying it. fxcss deliberately ships no scheduler of its own — this is the piece you point yours at.

The layout selected at install time (--subpath, --entry) is recorded and reused, so a theme taken from 2.WithTST/ is upgraded from 2.WithTST/ and one taken from src/userChrome-WhiteSur.css from the same edition.

$ fxcss upgrade fxcss upgrade default-release profile default-release ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/8f2h1kqp.default-release installed AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS @ v1.6.3 upstream v2.0.0 2026-08-16 fetching v2.0.0 … layout chrome/ at the repository root 72 stylesheets, 377 KB loads 35 stylesheets 29 browser-window, 2 web-content, 4 shared sheets keeping theme-nord Upgrade to v2.0.0? [Y/n] backup the previous version, kept as chrome.backup-20260817014202 ✓ Upgraded to v2.0.0 Restart Firefox to see it; fxcss rollback puts the previous version back.

title: fxcss rollback
description: Installs and upgrades that replace an existing chrome/ keep it as a chrome.backup-*. Managed backups include the installation record, so the list can show what…

search.text: Restore the newest backup, or choose one by name:
fxcss rollback fxcss rollback --list fxcss rollback --to chrome.backup-20260817014202
Installs and upgrades that replace an existing chrome/ keep it as a chrome.backup-*. Managed backups include the installation record, so the list can show what each one holds:

$ fxcss rollback --list fxcss rollback default-release profile default-release ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/8f2h1kqp.default-release installed AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS @ v2.0.0 Backups newest first chrome.backup-20260817014202 AdamXweb/WhiteSurFirefoxThemeMacOS@v1.6.3 chrome.backup-20260817014143 the original your own chrome/, from before fxcss fxcss rollback --to <name> restores one of these.

fxcss rollback restores the most recent, or --to <name> any of them. What was installed becomes a backup in its turn, so a rollback can itself be rolled back, and user.js follows: each version records the prefs it asked for, and rolling back to the original — the one backup with no manifest in it, because it is your chrome folder from before any of this — takes the fxcss pref block out with it.

That original is the reason upgrades chain rather than stack blindly. After five upgrades the newest backup holds the theme, not your files, so the manifest carries the original's name forward and fxcss uninstall still restores what you had before you ever ran fxcss. --keep N (default 3) prunes older backups; the original is never one of them, and neither is any chrome.backup-* folder that holds no fxcss install record.

title: fxcss uninstall
description: Removes the managed theme and its user.js preference block. Recorded files are removed only when their hashes still match; added, edited, unreadable or…

search.text: fxcss uninstall fxcss uninstall --profile default-release

Removes the managed theme and its user.js preference block. Recorded files are removed only when their hashes still match; added, edited, unreadable or unverifiable files are kept. If nothing needs to be retained, the original chrome/ backup is restored. Otherwise the backup stays alongside the retained files so it cannot overwrite your work.
If the profile originally had no chrome/, uninstalling after an upgrade returns it to that state when no files need to be kept. Restart Firefox to see the result.

A chrome/ with no manifest in it is yours — what a rollback to the original put back, or a theme installed by hand — and uninstall leaves it exactly as it is, however many backups sit beside it: it removes a leftover fxcss block from user.js if there is one, lists the backups, and changes nothing else. So install → rollback → uninstall ends with your original files in place, and running it again does the same. If chrome/ is absent after an interrupted swap or a completed uninstall, uninstall leaves that absent state alone too. Use fxcss rollback --to <backup-name> explicitly to restore a backup.

title: fxcss new
description: Creates a small working theme you can edit immediately. Save changes to chrome/userChrome.css while watch is running to see them in Firefox. Stop with Ctrl-C…

search.text: fxcss new my-theme cd my-theme fxcss watch

Creates a small working theme you can edit immediately. Save changes to chrome/userChrome.css while watch is running to see them in Firefox. Stop with Ctrl-C when you want to run another command. The starter is also used by fxcss's own browser tests; an existing non-empty directory is left alone.

title: fxcss watch

Opens Firefox with your theme applied and watches chrome/ and custom/. Save a CSS file in your editor and the running window reloads it automatically.
The window is yours to drive — open menus, resize it, type in the address bar, right-click things. Nothing is scripted.

flag effect --dark start in dark mode, for testing prefers-color-scheme rules --native-menus=false make right-click menus themeable (see Context menus) --shot out.png write a screenshot after every reload --no-devtools don't enable the Browser Toolbox

title: fxcss inspect
description: The same report, for a selector you already have. Useful for checking whether a selector still matches anything after a Firefox update — a common cause of…
